segments.text: The evals talk argued deflection is the wrong headline metric: containment without resolution flatters every vendor presenting.

Ninety seconds of Q&A mattered more than the slides. Someone asked whether the 70% deflection figure on screen counted tickets that went silent, and the speaker said yes, silence counts as containment in every benchmark they publish. The room laughed in the way rooms laugh when they already knew.

Contained tickets reopen about a fifth of the time within a week. CSAT is measured on contained tickets only, so the tickets that reopen never get surveyed. Nobody presenting would give a resolved-without-reopen number, which is itself the number.
[[Containment is not resolution]] has the paper version. For any ship review: ask what share of contained tickets stayed resolved, and who owns the ones that came back.

segments.text: Support-agent benchmarks overstate deflection: most count containment without checking resolution.

The paper defines containment as no human reply within 24 hours and resolution as the issue fixed with no reopen in seven days. Across eleven vendors, contained tickets reopened 18 to 26% of the time, and another 10 to 15% went silent with no CSAT either way. The headline deflection numbers vendors publish are containment numbers.

Ask for three numbers, not one: contained share, reopened-in-7d share, and resolved-without-reopen share. A 41% deflection figure with no reopen rate attached is a containment figure wearing a resolution costume. The paper's rule of thumb: discount published deflection by a third until the vendor shows reopen data.

The pilot counts containment exactly the way the paper warns about: no human reply in 24 hours. Ivy flagged the same gap in the eval setup. If the GA review opens with the 41%, open with the definition, then ask for the reopen rate before reacting. See also [[Evals talk notes]] for the conference version of the same argument.

segments.text: Staff across Compass, Tally and Northwind, and every decision is landing in the same week.

The reading backlog is the honest problem: forty open tabs on evals, retrieval and agents, read in fragments between reviews, connected to nothing. The knowledge is in here somewhere. It just never surfaces at the moment a decision needs it.

Compass wants a GA call Thursday with a 41% pilot number nobody has interrogated. Tally wants a retrieval design before the contracts freeze Friday. Northwind wants a launch ruling with two red-team findings open. Each one is reasonable alone. Together they mean every evening this week is prep.
One page per review: what the request says, what my own notes say about it, and the one question to open with. Not more reading. Less, at the right moment.

draft.question: Should Compass ship the support copilot?

sentences.text: The engineer's first tab is a note about which link they trust.
No, Compass should hold GA, because the plan expands from the measured pilot to a much broader launch while key open questions remain in the request itself.
The 41% headline is a containment number, not a resolution number, since the pilot counted containment when there was no human reply within 24 hours of the agent's final message.
The sampled resolution data does not support shipping yet, because only 63% were resolved without a reopen, while 22% reopened within seven days and 15% went silent among the 200 contained tickets.

The rollout risk is unresolved because approval is requested for all twelve queues, the request still raises whether 41% holds outside the three friendliest queues, and reopened tickets currently sit with no queue owner.

The right D0 briefing is to hold and require resolution-based evidence first, consistent with the eval warning that containment is cheap to measure and easy to game and that nobody had sampled whether contained tickets were actually resolved.
